abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Domestic, industrial, and agricultural wastewater contains higher concentration of pollutants, including carbon and nitrogen nutrients, heavy metals, and harmful chemicals, which significantly impact human health and the ecosystem. In this scenario, phycoremediation is an eco-friendly and economically viable technique that harnesses the diversity of algae to eliminate elevated carbon and nitrogen elements, as well as other contaminants in aquatic systems. Therefore, this review critically examines recent advancements in the utilization of algae for inland water and wastewater treatment applications, with a focus on carbon and nitrogen removal. Furthermore, this study examines the optimization of pollutant removal using different algae, algal consortium, and bacterial consortia for sustainable water management. Additionally, it highlights the feasibility of algae-based treatment, which enhances water quality while potentially producing biomass for biofuels and various high-value products. The challenges, recommendations, and future directions presented in this review can lay a roadmap for effectively selecting a resilient algal strain for phycoremediation of wastewater, thereby promoting environmental sustainability.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Water pollution has become a serious global concern, resulting from different industrial discharges, agricultural runoff, and untreated urban wastewater. Rapid industrialization and urbanization, coupled with insufficient awareness about water’s critical importance, have left approximately 80% of the global population vulnerable to water scarcity and contamination risks. Only about 2.5% of Earth’s water is fresh, out of which just 0.036% is readily accessible for our use; the remaining 1.96% is stored in polar ice caps, underground wells, and aquifers.1 This tiny portion of the freshwater ecosystem has also been significantly affected by human activities, and pollution has become a threat to both life and environmental health.2 Advanced scientific approaches are necessary for maintaining ecosystem health and promoting human well-being, necessitating education and awareness to mitigate risks and preserve this vital resource. Based on recent reports, 11 million tons of plastic enter water reservoir like oceans, rivers, and seas worldwide each year. These plastics can take up to 200 years to degrade. If the trend continues, the total amount of plastic could rise to around 29 million tons by 2040.3 On the other hand, the demand for freshwater is projected to increase by one-third globally by 2050. Therefore, there is an urgent need for proactive measures to address water scarcity and concerns about water quality. Recognizing the importance of these issues, developed countries, such as the US, have implemented certain measures over the past two decades, which reports suggest have shown substantial progress. This is mainly driven by significant increases in the wastewater collection and treatment capacities: exceeding 90% in both urban and rural areas.4 Moreover, in developed countries, nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus are the major contributors (30%–40%) to inland water pollution, originating from agricultural and urban sources. In contrast, in developing countries, this quantum is at much higher levels (up to 70%) due to less efficient agricultural practices and inadequate wastewater treatment.5 Worldwide, key water pollutants include organic pollutants (10%–20% in developed, similar in developing), heavy metals (5%–10% in developed, up to 30% in developing), pathogens (20%–30% in both), and sediments (10%–30% in both), where the relative contribution of each can vary based on differences in industrial practices and regulatory enforcements.6 Water pollution arises from multiple sources. Among them, industrial activities are the primary contributors to contaminating inland waters in all kinds of areas, including rural, urban, and semi-urban areas. Consequently, these activities are known to cause a range of environmental issues over both immediate and extended periods; their negative impacts on communities are also well-documented. In particular, the wastewater released by industries leads to substantial water pollution and poses health risks worldwide. It is reported that each year, industries consume around 865 km3 of freshwater from a total of 3,928 km3. When industrial effluents are insufficiently treated before being released into sewerage systems, they can contaminate groundwater and harm aquatic life. Moreover, these pollutants exacerbate several other environmental problems, including air and soil contamination. This untreated wastewater may make its way into agricultural use, which can damage crops and introduce harmful contaminants into the food supply. The origin of many waterborne illnesses, such as diarrhea, giardiasis, typhoid fever, cholera, hepatitis, jaundice, and cancer, can be traced to such contaminants. Wastewater generated from various sectors can be classified into several types, including sewage, domestic, storm runoff, agricultural, and industrial wastewater.7 In India, 17,000 highly polluting industries collectively discharge over 88,000 million liters of wastewater daily. In urban areas, only about 30% of this wastewater is treated before being released into a water body, whereas in rural areas, treatment facilities are still lacking, and the untreated water has been repeatedly cited as a reason for significant pollution.8 Inland waters are increasingly threatened by heavy metals, microplastics, and organic pollutants, as these are toxic, persistent, and detrimental to both water quality and human health. Effective management of these contaminants is essential for a comprehensive understanding of their sources, environmental behavior, and interactions. Pervasive microplastics exacerbate pollution by carrying organic and inorganic contaminants such as heavy metals and pesticides, emphasizing the need for sustainable strategies that balance environmental protection with economic growth.9 Inland water bodies are affected by multiple pollution sources: from industrial discharges (20%) to agricultural runoff (40%), including nitrogen and phosphorus, and urban sources (25%), such as sewage and stormwater, as well as mining activities (10%) releasing heavy metals and the increasingly prominent climate change impacts (5%) altering nutrient cycles. Therefore, protecting water quality and ecosystem health demands integrated strategies and the implementation of advanced technologies.10 The literature shows that many countries are directing their efforts into water treatment to address water scarcity and pollutant removal, as the focus on effective wastewater management has intensified with population growth and expanding industrialization. Wastewater treatment is also essential for recovering clean water and enabling the sustainable reuse of water resources.11 The treatment of inland water and industrial wastewater is crucial for protecting public health, preserving ecosystems, ensuring water security, and fostering economic growth. Untreated inland water serves as a major source of waterborne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, and dysentery, which collectively affect over 2 billion people globally and cause approximately 1.4 million deaths annually. A proper wastewater treatment safeguards drinking water sources, maintains aquatic balance, and supports wetlands by preventing eutrophication and biodiversity loss.12 Further, it promotes water reuse in agriculture and industry, reducing freshwater demand by 30%–40% and supporting economic stability through efficient resource use. Exploring the potential of sundry algal species for phycoremediation of both inland water and different types of wastewaters imparts an inclusive and complete comprehension of water treatment to the readers. Eco-technologies like phycoremediation offer dual benefits by removing up to 83%–96% heavy metals and 43%–100%, emerging pollutants while enabling resource recovery in the form of biofuels, biofertilizers, and biopolymers making it a cost-effective and sustainable wastewater management approach.13

Most of the conventional N removal proposed using solid carbon source like sugarcane bagasse. One study with supplementing intermittently aerated constructed wetlands (CWs), significantly enhanced nitrogen removal, achieving 98.3% total N removal at an influent C/N ratio of 5 with sugarcane bagasse fermentation liquid (SBFL), and outperformed sucrose in NO3--N and NH4+-N removal. The addition of SBFL further reduce N2O emissions by 17.8%–43.7% and maintained low CH4 emissions.14 Even though conventional treatment is an easy approach, it limited their effectiveness against certain pollutants like heavy metals, high operational costs, energy intensity, chemical dependency, challenges in sludge disposal, and limited adaptability to changing environmental conditions, necessitating exploration of alternative and integrated approaches for more sustainable water management.15 Interest in green wastewater treatments is growing, with methods including phycoremediation (using algae), CWs, biological filtration, bioaugmentation, membrane bioreactors (MBRs), anaerobic digestion, aquaponics, and natural systems such as oxidation ponds. These promising approaches for sustainably decontaminating and restoring ecosystems while minimizing harm to biodiversity.16 Phycoremediation treats elements such as phosphorus, nitrogen, sulfur, and minerals as nutrients for algal growth, rather than contaminants; this alternative approach is key to removing pollutants like nitrates, phosphates, agrochemicals, hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and excess nitrogen and phosphorus from water bodies. Apart from phycoremediation, some other green wastewater treatment like phytoremediation17 (plants like Brassica juncea, Willow trees and Vetiver grass) and mycoremediation (fungi like Oyster mushrooms, Pleurotus ostreatus and White-rot fungus, Phanerochaete chrysosporium) were also reported by many researchers.18 In phytoremediation, pollutants such as heavy metals, pesticides, hydrocarbons, and chlorinated solvents are removed through three main mechanisms: accumulation, degradation, and stabilization. In mycoremediation, the fungi remove pollutants through enzymatic degradation using extracellular enzymes and biosorption via their mycelial network.19 Further, because of shallow root depth, slow growth rates, and the need for biomass disposal the phytoremediation is limited for large scale promotion.20 While mycoremediation faces challenges like environmental sensitivity, uneven fungal growth, and difficulty in large-scale application.21 In contrast, phycoremediation, uses microalgae and cyanobacteria, which offer faster and more efficient pollutant removal, adaptability to aquatic systems, and the added benefit of nutrient recovery and biomass valorization, making it a more sustainable and versatile remediation approach.22 The approach of phycoremediation for inland/wastewater treatment is shown in Figure 1.

sec.p: The phycoremediation technique also inhibits bacterial proliferation, enhancing water disinfection.23 Additionally, it reduces PO4-P, NH3-N, and COD concentrations in primary-treated effluent by approximately 97.89%, 98.81%, and 88.24%, respectively, demonstrating its strong eco-friendly treatment potential.24 Many researchers have discussed with various algal species like Chlorella, Scenedesmus, Spirulina, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, Nannochloropsis, Dunaliella, and Euglena for water treatment. These microalgae play a crucial role in removing nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, which significantly contribute to cleaning the water. Among them, Spirulina and Chlorella are known for their potential for biomass production, while Phaeodactylum tricornutum is preferred for lipid production. Dunaliella can survive even in high-salinity environments, and Euglena is also considered a promising potential bioenergy source. Additionally, Microalgae provide a sustainable solution for improving the quality of landfill leachate while producing useful biomass. In a recent study, textile wastewater (TWW) was treated with Chlorella vulgaris (CV) and algal biomass carbon (algal-BC), with the aim of achieving environmental conservation while creating an additional avenue for energy production. In BC helps to increase the adsorption of pollutants and also provides nutrients that support the growth of microalgae, leading to higher biomass productivity and carbon capture (77.57 ± 2.52 mg L−1 day−1).25 A CV-BC-TWW system was demonstrated to achieve over 99% bioremediation by removing pollutants such as MB, COD, nitrates, and phosphates through biosorption and biodegradation processes. Furthermore, this method can be extended to value-added development in bioremediation. This integrated approach also improves biodiesel production (up to 76.79 ± 2.01 mg g−1) due to enriched fatty acid profiles; therefore, it can serve as a sustainable and efficient approach for wastewater treatment and energy generation.26 A recent review emphasizes the remediation of contaminants such as hydrocarbons, pesticides, radioactive substances, and heavy metals from wastewater,27 and it provides an overview of phycoremediation where microalgae are used to clean wastewater by removing pollutants, particularly heavy metals (HMs). Furthermore, the review also discusses various strategies, including rhizofiltration, CWs, algal mats, and waste stabilization ponds, explaining how they enhance water quality by utilizing algae and valorizing algal biomass for biofuel, animal feed, and fertilizers. It also mentions several new biotechnological approaches, such as genetic modifications and metabolic engineering, that can enhance the efficiency and specificity of phycoremediation processes.27 However, unlike that review, our proposed review majorly focuses on phycoremediation, particularly on how algae/cyanobacteria remove of carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) nutrients from wastewater, thus prioritizing nutrient pollution control. In addition, this review examines recent advancements in phycoremediation technologies and outlines their underlying mechanisms for carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) assimilation. It highlights the dual benefits of phycoremediation: (i) effective water purification and (ii) valuable biomass generation via circular economy models. This review also stands out because it addresses resource recovery from wastewater and compares different processes of converting algal biomass into biofuels and high-value bioproducts; hence, this brings out the environmental and economic advantages of algal-based remediation systems. Microalgae are emerged as a promising bioresource for producing high-value products such as proteins, fatty acids, pigments, anti-aging compounds, and bioenergy, owing to their exceptional biomass productivity and nutrient removal capacity. Their cultivation using wastewater offers sustainable, non-competitive resource utilization, presenting vast opportunities for commercial bioindustry development.28 High-value by-products like polysaccharides, pigments, bioactive compounds, and energy products like hydrogen and methane are derived from phycoremediation. High-value chemicals typically offer greater economic returns per unit biomass (up to $5,000–$10,000/ton) but have limited market scale, whereas energy products provide lower economic margins (around $200–$600/ton of algal dry weight) yet support large-scale circular bioeconomy applications through renewable fuel generation and carbon recycling. A recent study reports that, with basic strains Chlorella, Chlamydomonas, and Scenedesmus are ideally suited for phycoremediation, they produce the by-products high protein and lipid contents, biofuel, H2, and electricity generation.23

Overall, this review takes a forward-looking view on sustainable inland water and wastewater treatment by diverse algal species. Further, significance of temperature, pH, and light intensity on the phycoremediation potential will be discussed as these factors influence algal growth rates and biomass productivity and are seen as crucial for optimizing C and N removal efficiency and other integrated applications. A separate section was presented on biofuels and various high-value products extraction from wastewater tolerant algal biomass.

sec.title: Phycoremediation and significance of algae
sec.p: In wastewater treatment, various strategies are used to remove nutrients. These typically include biological processes, chemical precipitation methods for removing phosphorus, adsorption techniques which use materials like activated carbon, as well as membrane-based technologies and wetland constructions. These methods are effective for nitrogen and phosphorus, and they catering to diverse treatment needs and environmental conditions.29 Conventional methods for nutrient removal in wastewater treatment, such as aerobic activated sludge processes and chemical phosphorus removal, often face several limitations. They tend to consume large amounts of energy, exhibit unstable treatment, and show poor efficiencies in resource recovery. These shortcomings run counter to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, which emphasize reducing carbon emissions and calls for better use of resources.30 In this regard, a method more in line with these goals is phycoremediation, a technique that employs microalgae for efficient removal of carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) from polluted water bodies. Microalgae are highly versatile organisms with potential applications in areas such as pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and effluent water treatment, as they are known for to their rapid growth and adaptability to varied, even extreme, environments, from deserts to cold climates. Further, algal biomass is rich in valuable compounds like proteins and lipids, making them valuable for many industries.31,32 Microalgae absorb CO2 during photosynthesis. In the process, the final products are biomass and oxygen. This process is key to reducing carbon emissions and improving water quality, as well as being important in the uptake of nitrogen compounds in the soil, like nitrate (NO3−) and ammonium (NH4+), and in the water by mitigating eutrophication through nitrogen reduction. The latter process can occur through direct assimilation into cellular components or together with bacteria that facilitate denitrification.33 This approach offers a more sustainable method for removing nutrients, as it relies on natural biological processes. Although these processes occur naturally, they can be adjusted or optimized based on our understanding of individual algal species and their surrounding environmental conditions. As a heterotrophic organism, algae convert inorganic nutrients into biomass using solar energy. Previous research has reported productivity of algal reactors to be ranging from 40 to 150 tons/ha·year (dry matter) depending on design parameters and environmental factors.34 According to one recent study, achieving high productivity requires considerable amounts of inputs: up to 200 tons of CO2, 10 tons of nitrogen (N), and 1 ton of phosphorus (P) per 100 tons of biomass. In terms of cost, the study notes that these inputs are typically supplied as chemical fertilizers costing around 0.5 €/kg.35 Another study utilized flue gases and wastewater as nutrient sources with the aim of reducing associated costs, thus improving the chances of profitability by recovering valuable nutrients. The integration of microalgae cultivation with wastewater treatment has been extensively investigated for various effluents, including sewage and manure. The main of aim of such integration is to reclaim nitrogen and phosphorus as biomass. Reported biomass production yields can be up to 1 kg of dry microalgae per m3 of sewage and over 10 kg per m3 of manure. These figures highlight microalgal role in nutrient recovery technologies.36 Most of the compounds present in wastewater are subsequently released into the atmosphere, primarily as carbon as CO2 and nitrogen as N2. Phosphorus, on the other hand, typically precipitates; it then needs to be removed with the digested sludge.37 According to a study, conventional wastewater treatment methods can cost as much as 0.2 €/m3 and require approximately 0.5 kWh/m3 of energy, while also releasing CO2 and nitrogen. FCC Aqualia processes 500 Mm3 annually, resulting in the emission of 1,000 kt CO2, 25 kt nitrogen, and 5 kt phosphorus—equivalent to Fertiberia’s fertilizer production. Adopting microalgae cultivation has the potential to generate 500 kilotons of biomass per year, significantly cutting CO2 emissions and saving more than 50% of the energy compared to conventional methods.11 Microalgal biomass production is influenced by solar radiation and the efficiency of photosynthesis. Solar radiation typically ranges from 150 to 350 W/m2 annually, which impacts algal growth. Photosynthetic efficiency can vary from 1% in open systems to 5% under optimized conditions.38 Also, the CO2 fixation capacity spans 40 to 200 t/ha year in low solar areas and 70 to 450 t/ha·year in tropical regions, while nitrogen recovery ranges from 2 to 10 t/ha·year and phosphorus from 0.2 to 1.1 t/ha·year in less sunny regions; tropical areas see 5 to 25 tN/ha·year and 0.5 to 2.5 tP/ha·year38,39 More researches were carried out with nutrients removal and by product development using microalgae. A study reported microalgae and microalgae–bacteria consortia are efficient for CO2 fixation from waste gases, wastewater treatment, and producing value-added products. Also, mixed cultures and consortia enhance biomass yield and nutrient removal efficiency compared to monocultures.40 Microalgae such as Chlorella sp., Pediastrum sp., Scenedesmus sp., and Phormidium sp., among others, are commonly applied, with most strains belonging to Cyanophyta and Chlorophyta. The bacteria present in microalgae–bacteria consortia mainly come from activated sludge and particular sewage sources, integrating the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle in microalgae boost CO2 fixation and product yield.41 Compared to all nutrients, an efficient carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) removal from wastewater is crucial due to their environmental impacts. Previous studies reported nitrogen removal efficiencies in wastewater treatment plants range from 60% to 90%, impacting water quality and aquatic life (Environmental Protection Agency [EPA], 2023). Excess nitrogen, above 10 mg/L in drinking water, poses health risks like methemoglobinemia in infants (WHO, 2022). Carbon removal, up to 80% in treatment plants, helps mitigate greenhouse gas emissions (USEPA, 2021).42 Generally, in aqueous environments, nitrogen exists as inorganic (NH3, NH4+, NO2−, NO3−, and N2) and organic compounds (amino acids, amino sugars, urea, proteins, uric acid). NH3 and NH4+ equilibrium depends on pH. NO2− is unstable and toxic, quickly oxidizing to NO3−. The carbon (C) to nitrogen (N) ratio is crucial in wastewater treatment as it directly impacts microbial activity and nutrient removal efficiency. Maintaining a balanced C ratio, typically around 20–30:1, promotes optimal microbial growth for effective organic matter degradation and nitrogen assimilation.44 One study investigated the impact of varying N/P ratios (5–30) on biomass growth and nutrient removal from municipal wastewaters using an optical panel photobioreactor (PBR). However, TP removal depends significantly on both N/P ratio and biomass productivity, indicating optimal ratios between 5 and 30 for efficient wastewater treatment.45 Another study optimized a microalgae-based treatment using Scenedesmus obliquus under various agitation and aeration conditions. This aeration enhanced biomass and chlorophyll-a content (725.32–811.16 × 104 cells mL−1, 1.58–1.69 mg L−1) compared to agitation (426.06–465.14 × 104 cells mL−1, 1.48–1.61 mg L−1). Nutrient removal efficiencies were higher in sucrose wastewater under agitation (TP 1.84–2.30 mg L−1, TN 29.62–36.39 mg L−1, 21.33%–30.67% and 44.84%–58.51%, respectively, on day 2) and in both sucrose and humic acid wastewater under aeration (TN 19.56–31.20 mg L−1, TP 0.26–0.30 mg L−1, 13.92%–46.75% and 88.36%–90.50%, respectively, on day 5). Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in the wastewater consisted mainly of humic-like substances, with higher aromaticity and humification in humic acid conditions affecting pollutant removal by algae. This study provides insights for optimizing coupled with other processes.46 Heterotrophic cultivation of Phormidium autumnale in sugarcane vinasse, shows promise due to high biomass yield and contaminant removal. Cultivation at 35°C with a C/N ratio of 16 and pH 7.5 achieved biomass productivity of 127.20 mg L−1 day−1, removing 49% organic carbon, 47% nitrogen, and 28% phosphorus. Batch cultivation improved organic carbon (67%) and nitrogen (70%) removal, with significant bioproducts: 4.26% lipids, 197.53 mg g−1 phycocyanin, 21.33% proteins, and various carbohydrates suitable for exopolysaccharides. P. autumnale effectively treats vinasse, yielding valuable bioproducts alongside wastewater purification.47 A research study reported that biochar derived from Chlorella vulgaris loaded with nZVI (BC/nZVI) reduced algal toxicity, lowering growth inhibition from 98.10% (nZVI) to 42.86%, and mitigating pigment loss (chlorophyll a 62.66%, b 58.84%, carotenoids 45.74%) and oxidative stress (SOD 163.13 U/mg, MDA 73.84 nmol/mg). Overall, BC/nZVI exhibited high reactivity with reduced toxicity, making it suitable for eco-friendly pollutant remediation.48 Further, the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are toxic emerging pollutants causing reproductive, endocrine, and carcinogenic effects in living organisms. It can be removed effectively by microalgae or consortium with bacteria/fungi, offer an eco-friendly and efficient alternative to conventional PAH. Integration of genetic engineering, nanotechnology, and AI/ML tools further enhances the effectiveness of microalgal based bioremediation.49

sec.title: Reactors used in phycoremediation
sec.p: The key factors that govern bioreactor performance to enhance pollutant removal efficacy are light intensity, nutrient availability, temperature and pH. Maintaining optimal pH and hydraulic retention time ensures effective algae activity and biomass productivity. The reactor design, including surface area and mixing mechanisms, plays a critical role in maximizing remediation effectiveness.50 Different types of reactors used in algae-based water treatment, namely the conventional activated sludge (CAS), MBR, bio discs sewage treatment, bio-filters, trickling filters moving bed biofilm reactor (MBBR).51 Further, a sustainable water treatment approach extended by algae-based membrane bioreactors (AMBRs), which effectively removes pharmaceuticals, antibiotics, and hydrocarbons, outperforming traditional treatment plants.52 A recent study, reports A novel microalgae membrane bioreactor integrated with an internal circulating fluidized bed demonstrated high treatment efficiency for marine aquaculture wastewater, which achieving NO3−-N of 52%, 85% of NH4+-N, and 80% PO43−-P removal.53 Another study with AMBR with osmotic membrane (OMPBR) under tertiary wastewater attained the removal of TN, 99% and TP, 100%.54 Different wastewater treatment strategies for nutrient recovery are shown in Figure 2.

sec.p: Generally, an activated sludge process efficiently treats wastewater using aerobic microorganisms in aeration tanks. It consumes organic matter, achieving high treatment efficiency, followed by effective settling and clarification of the effluent for clean water output. One study discussed, with microalgal-bacterial symbiotic system in SBR achieved, 100% removal of ammonium, high COD removal, and optimal nutrient removal (TN 53.85%, TP 85.13%) with 5:1 algae to sludge ratio. COD removal was consistently high across ratios. It also enriches the Comamonadaceae, Flavobacterium, Paenarthrobacter, Mesorhizobium, and Nitrobacter and highlighting their role in nutrient degradation and symbiosis dynamics during different stages of the reaction.55 Another study reported that a symbiotic co-culture of microalgae and activated sludge, co-culture achieved up to 93% nitrate (NO3−) and 99% phosphate (PO4−) removal, along with 73% COD reduction, with a maximum biomass yield of 7.8 g/L.56 Despite its benefits, such as effective nutrient removal and organic matter reduction, it has several limitations, including high energy consumption for aeration, sensitivity to shock loads that impact treatment efficiency, excess sludge production necessitating disposal, potential odors, and susceptibility to process upsets that affect water quality.57 Further, algae in PBRs efficiently remove pollutants like nitrogen, phosphorus, and heavy metals from wastewater, aiding in environmental cleanup. This system utilized Desmodesmus sp., a green microalgae strain that was originally isolated for this purpose. To enhance nutrient uptake rate, a low cell concentration was maintained during light inhibition periods. Strategies included cell mass recycling during high light availability and adjusting dilution rates. Compared to conventional methods, these strategies increased biomass productivity by 80% in summer and 10% in winter, whereas nitrogen/phosphorus (N/P) removal rates improved by 23% during winter and remained stable in summer.25 Another study with Scenedesmus obliquus in rice mill paddy-soaked wastewater (PSW) PBR demonstrated superior performance with maximum biomass productivity (340 ± 2 mg/L/d), NH3-N removal (96.12 ± 0.21%), and PO4-P removal (97.58 ± 0.18%). PBR also yielded the highest lipid (L ∼12% of biomass), protein (P ∼40%), and carbohydrate (C ∼20%) content compared to raceway ponds and polybags.58 Furthermore, the research extended to paper industry wastewater, which was treated using a consortium of Chlorella sp., Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter calcoaceticus in a batch PBR, achieving a biomass productivity of 3.17 g/L. Removal efficiencies reached 99.95% for total nitrogen and 95.16% for COD, highlighting effective wastewater treatment by the microalgae-bacteria consortium.59 Regarding reactor optimization, the CAS is commonly used as a biological stage in wastewater treatment, which can be easily and effectively integrated with algae culturing units, such as algal ponds, to enhance nutrient removal. The highest removals were observed as 84% DOC under blue light at 300 μmol/m2·s, and 51% DN and 80% DP under red light at 100 μmol/m2·s.60 The energy ranges limited between 0.18 and 0.8 kWh·m−3, aligning with typical wastewater treatment plant values of 0.35–0.65 kWh·m−3. In open raceway ponds (ORPs), the energy demand is 0.10–0.35 kWh m−3 with light energy utilization as 80–250 μmol photons m−2 s−1. Due to its simple construction, it has low CAPEX and OPEX, at nearly 1.98 and 9.69 EUR/kg. However, it is susceptible to contamination and weather fluctuations.61 Furthermore, regarding the high-rate algal pond (HRAP), which operates under 150–400 μmol photons·m−2·s−1 mixed light with an energy consumption of 0.29 kWh·m−3, this system has higher algal growth at a lower cost of €0.04 per m−3.62 A recent study reported an energy consumption of 0.02 kWh/m3 for HRAPs compared to 0.20–0.4 kWh/m3 for activated sludge.63 Closed PBRs are the best alternatives for open ponds, which operate with light intensity of 60–700 μmol m−2 s−, also they offer precise control over environmental and operational parameters.64 A study reports that a twisted tubular PBR design would reduce energy consumption by 38% compared to actual tubular PBR conditions.65 However, their high energy requirements for maintaining optimal conditions significantly increase overall operational costs.

A study reported with Chlorella vulgaris and native sludge bacteria consortium in batch PBRs at 24°C under continuous light achieved approximately 75% removal of total phosphorus and total nitrogen, alongside biohydrogen production rates ranging from 35% to 40%66 Another study cultivated three cyanobacterial strains namely Anabaena oryzae, Nostoc muscorum, and Spirulina platensis, were cultivated in potato industry wastewater and synthetic media. The highest growth rates were observed in the mixed cyanobacterial culture and Spirulina platensis in PIW, achieving chlorophyll contents of 3.75 and 2.30 μg·mL−1, DWs of 1.79 g·L−1, and 1.63 g L−1, and ODs of 0.41 and 0.38, respectively.67 The analysis of the lipid profile showed that the fatty acid methyl ester composition was well-suited for biodiesel production. This finding highlights the potential of C. vulgaris in mitigating environmental impacts resulting from dairy wastewater.68 Furthermore, an algal membrane PBR (AMBR) wastewater treatment with Chlorella vulgaris was investigated to reduce land use, shorten retention times, minimize fouling, and ensure efficient biomass separation, achieving substantial biomass of nearly 7.37 g/m2 and a lipid content of nearly 10.17%.25 Another study with greywater treatment using algal biomass, peaked at 48 mg/L/d with HRT, while maintaining high removal efficiencies: 94% for BOD and 96% for anionic surfactants. The highest total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) removals are 59.5% and 34.5%, respectively. HRT, the system achieved the highest methane yield of 0.332 m3/d and net energy return (NER) of 1.04, suggesting self-sustainability with zero power requirements.69 Another experiment with mixed bioreactors showed significant improvements in biomass production and phycoremediation of secondary urban effluent, with notable reductions in biological oxygen demand (54.34%), total phosphorus (92.4%), ammoniacal nitrogen (97.1%), and total Kjeldahl nitrogen (92.8%). Furthermore, CO2 enhances microalgal growth and cell density by 54.26% in a shorter time. Biomass yields were 0.5324 ± 0.007 g L−1 without CO2 and 0.821 ± 0.014 g L−1 with CO2.70 Furthermore, this study extends to a flat panel PBR for the mixotrophic treatment of dairy wastewater using Tetradesmus sp. SVMIICT4, achieving effective COD and nutrient removal. The biomass accumulated carbohydrate (21.48 mg g−1) and protein (19.52 mg g−1). Also, it Increased chlorophyll content nearly 18.94 mg g−1, enhanced electron transport (ET/Rc) and reduced non-photochemical quenching (NPQ).71 Raceway ponds (RWPs), another type of reactor used in phycoremediation, are characterized by circular or rectangular channels with paddlewheel circulation. These ponds strike a balance between cost-effectiveness and operational efficiency, making them suitable for larger-scale applications. Additionally, the controlled movement of algae cultures in the ponds promotes nutrient absorption and biomass production. A study reported that when impregnated activated charcoal (IAC) was used along with algal species such as Spirogyra and C. pyrenoidosa in RWPs, the system achieved more than 75.7% TN removal. Winter-spring seasons showed higher nitrogen removal, affirming both systems’ effectiveness in mitigating eutrophication from sewage.72 Another study with an 800 L scale inland pond using a native algae consortium effectively removed nutrients, such as ammonia, nitrate, phosphate, and COD, within safe discharge limits in both batch and raceway ponds. The harvested algal biomass was lipid-rich (45.87% total solids, TS). Anaerobic digestion revealed a theoretical methane potential of 745.87 mL CH4 g−1 VS, with an experimental yield of up to 630 mL CH4 g−1 VS.73 A comparative study with anaerobically digested piggery effluent (ADPE) using a thin layer reactor (TLR) and a raceway pond reported with Chlorella sp. and Scenedesmus sp, exhibited a higher ammonium removal rate of 19.23 mg N-NH4+ L−1 day−1) compared to the raceway pond. The ash-free biomass yield is 0.84 g L−1, and the average volumetric biomass productivity is 60 mg L−1 day−1, which is significantly higher by 2–2.5 times in the TLR. However, due to its larger volume, the raceway pond achieved higher areal biomass productivity nearly 4.2 g m−2 day−1, resulting in 2.7 times higher areal lipid productivity than the TLR. Overall, the raceway pond outperformed the TLR for ADPE treatment based on areal biomass productivity under operational conditions.74

sec.title: Wastewater treatment/inland water treatment by diverse algal species
sec.p: Generally, the nutrient recovery from water depends on the nature of the species and environmental conditions. Numerous studies have been carried out to explore optimal cellular characteristics and strategies for enhancing water treatment. These investigations focus on understanding the factors such as nutrient availability, light intensity, and temperature conditions. Wastewater and inland water treatment using various algal species involves exploiting their ability to uptake nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus, thereby reducing the concentration of pollutants in the water. Algal species such as Chlorella, Scenedesmus, and Spirulina are some of the commonly employed ones, as they have been found to be efficient in nutrient uptake and biomass production. These species show great potential for water purification and eutrophication control, as the algal photosynthesis can improve water quality, supporting ecological balance and sustainable resource management.75 Phycoremediation uses microalgae to bioremediate pollutants like NO3−, PO4−, and heavy metals from wastewater (WW) sustainably without generating hazardous byproducts. The technique can be a robust alternative to conventional treatments, as it offers the advantages of being cost-effective and eco-friendly, which go a long way in shrinking the carbon footprint. Efforts include immobilization techniques, pretreatment strategies, genetic engineering, and synergistic technologies to maximize phycoremediation and produce value-added products like bioenergy application.27,76 Diatoms excel in wastewater remediation and carbon dioxide capture, while yielding valuable products. Diatom biorefinery offers sustainable wastewater management, producing biomass for biofuels, biofertilizers, animal feed supplements, and pharmaceuticals rich in EPA, DHA, and pigments like fucoxanthin.77 Most of researches were focuses to maximize biomass yield, which serves as a valuable feedstock for various applications including biodiesel production, protein extraction, and biofertilizer development after wastewater treatment. Examination of the amino acids, peptides and fatty acids, derived from microalgae harvested in a pilot-scale phycoremediation of swine wastewater. The system reached a peak microalga concentration of 247 ± 3.4 mg L−1 and achieved complete removal of phosphate and ammonium. Also, it revealed high levels (% of total protein) of leucine (4.1), lysine (2.5), phenylalanine (2.6), and threonine (2.4) in amino acids. Fatty acids included 5.3% polyunsaturated (C18:2 and C18:3) and ∼10% monounsaturated (C16:1 and C18:1).78 One recent study evaluated pollutant removal like COD, TSS, NO3-N, turbidity, P using Chlorella vulgaris in livestock effluent with closed cultivation of 5 L bottles, 100%, 75%, 50%, 25% dilutions (to meet NWQS class II standards for recreational water). Results revealed that 61.97% TSS, 39.1% COD, and 36.4% P removal, respectively.79 Hypersaline pickled mustard wastewater was bioremediated using Chaetoceros muelleri and an indigenous bacterium. Reduction of 82% in COD, 90% in ammonia nitrogen, 94% in total nitrogen, and 96% in total phosphorus were achieved in 10% PMW. Microbial analysis showed increased abundance of Halomonas and Marinobacter, facilitating nutrient recycling by diatoms.80 The use of Chloroccocum humicola and Oscillatoria sp. for nutrient removal and lipid production revealed nutrient recovery rates ranged from 69.98% to 93.72% for phosphorus and 50.55%–85.90% for nitrogen. Heavy metal removal ranged from 24.17% to 88.10% across different wastewater concentrations (25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%). C. humicola effectively reduced physico-chemical parameters at 25% and 50% concentrations and achieved a notable 1.61-fold increase in lipid production at a 50% wastewater concentration.81 Another study investigated with integrated approaches with Chlorella minutissima and Chlorella sorokiniana in wastewater, and it reported Chlorella sorokiniana exhibited 19.14% higher lipids than Chlorella minutissima. Also, the biodiesel derived from Chlorella sorokiniana met USA and European standards (89.23 ± 0.21% lipid content). Both species effectively removed total phosphate (TP), total nitrogen (TN), chemical oxygen demand (COD), and total organic carbon (TOC) from wastewater, with TOC removal efficiencies of 95% and 98% for Chlorella minutissima and Chlorella sorokiniana, respectively.82 Further, phycoremediation potential of Chlorella vulgaris is demonstrated with industrial waste water to remove nutrients like 88.6% NH4-N and 91.2% PO4-P removal in synthetic wastewater, and effective reduction of NH4-N (68.6%), NO3-N (74%), PO4-P (71.5%), and COD (90.2%) in secondary treated sewage.83 Another study found that Chlorella fusca cell density was highest in treatments with 50% wastewater concentration, followed by 100%, 75%, the control, and 25%. BOD showed a 75% reduction at 100% wastewater addition. DOC levels decreased by 41% and 40% in 50% wastewater and 100% wastewater, respectively, while total nitrogen (TN) dropped by 55% at a 50% wastewater level.84 Another study reported that Chlorella fusca cell density increased in treatments with 50% urban wastewater (UW) concentration, followed by the treatment with 100% UW, 75% UW, the control, and finally 25% UW. Additionally, the protein content increased to 50.5% at a 75% UW concentration. Stress induced in microalgal cultures favored an increase in lipid production, reaching a maximum of 16.7% at a 100% UW concentration. The biological oxygen demand (BOD5) analysis indicated a 75% decrease in 100% UW concentration. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) levels decreased by 41% and 40% in 50% UW and 100% UW concentration, and total nitrogen (TN) decreased by 55% in 50% UW concentration.85 Further the nutrient removal can be enhanced using consortium cultivation.86 Six microalgal species, namely Scenedesmus abundans, Chlorella vulgaris, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, Coelastrum microporum, Nannochloropsis salina, and Dunaliella tertiolecta, were used for remediation of municipal wastewater reverse osmosis concentrate (ROC). It observed that S. abundans, C. vulgaris, and N. salina showed promise under salinity stress, N. salina adapted well to ROC conditions, while S. abundans demonstrated superior growth and salinity tolerance compared to C. vulgaris. Both S. abundans and N. salina effectively removed nutrients and organic matter by 11.5–18 mg/L/d TN, 7.1–8.2 mg/L/d TP, 8.6–12.4 mg/L/d DOC. Also, biochemical methane potential tests indicated significant methane production from algal biomass up to 422 mL CH4/g VS for N. salina, highlighting its potential for energy production via anaerobic digestion without requiring pretreatment.87 Another study assessed with Chlorella vulgaris efficacy in treating municipal wastewater, using primary treated effluent from a sewage treatment plant. Non-filtered effluent removal efficiencies of 98.32% for phosphate, 97.26% for ammonia, and 84.71% for COD was lower than filtered effluent i.e., 98.53% for phosphate, 98.63% for ammonia, and 89.41% for COD.88 The Chlamydomonas reinhardtii demonstrated the optimum performance and TP removal from 2 mg L−1 to 0.02 mg L−1. It significantly reduced TP and TN in domestic wastewater, achieving removal efficiencies up to 99.15% and 99.07%, respectively. For TN, reductions from 18.35 to 0.17 mg L−1 were observed in both C. reinhardtii and Chlorella pyrenoidosa. All microalgae strains produced lipids-rich biomass in wastewater exceeding BG11, with Chlorella sorokiniana recording the highest lipid content at 36.93%. FAME profiles revealed notable concentrations of palmitic acid, oleic acid, and stearic acid across the studied strains.89 Few investigations are focused on by product developments, in a study, glycerol supplementation at 3 g/L in synthetic wastewater boosted lipid accumulation in Chlorella pyrenoidosa by 133.74% (30.76% dry wt. basis) compared to controls without glycerol (13.16%). It also enhanced nutrient removal, with reductions of 96.35% in phosphate, 47.22% in nitrate, and 79.88% in COD over 15 days. Additionally, the microalgae produced 457.80 mg/L of exopolysaccharides, underscoring its dual potential for biomass enhancement and bioproduct synthesis through wastewater treatment.90

sec.title: Nutrient removal from different water reservoirs and wastewaters
sec.p: Various types of wastewater reservoirs include industrial effluent ponds, municipal sewage treatment lagoons, agricultural runoff retention basins, and natural wetlands. Each environment presents unique advantages and disadvantages for using plants to improve water quality by removing pollutants such as heavy metals, organic compounds, and excess nutrients. One study reported with Microalgae treatment in food processing plants, it obtained the biomass productivity up to 50% higher than terrestrial plants, also effectively removing pollutants like carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus by 40%–95%. Additionally, microalgae biomass can yield valuable metabolites, including pigments, amino acids, proteins, and unsaturated lipids. Residual biomass from extraction processes can be repurposed for energy generation and other valuable products.91 Another study assessed mushroom farm wastewater (MFW) treatment using microalga Chlamydomonas asymmetrica strain SAG70.72 isolated from the Ganga River, with 0%, 50%, and 100% MFW showed significant reductions (p < 0.05) in TDS (87%), BOD (93%), COD (92%), TKN (87%), and TP (97%) in 50% MFW. C. asymmetrica in 50% MFW also exhibited highest proximate, biochemical, and fatty acids methyl esters (FAMEs) composition. Also, this study reported, the first-order kinetic model indicated the highest rate constant (k), and logistic model best simulated its growth, suggesting potential for mitigating environmental impacts from mushroom cultivation.92 The study aimed to enhance heavy metals phycoextraction by diluting TE with harvested rainwater (HR) for Phragmites australis, supported by Oedogonium sp. and Pithophora sp. algae. Higher heavy metal uptake in treatment experimental devices TEDs with combined treatments compared to controls, supported by higher bioaccumulation factors. Biomass of P. australis was greater in TEDs with algae. HM translocation factor (TF) for Cr, Cu, Cd, and Pb remained ≥1, indicating effective phytoextraction.93 Another study examined Spirulina platensis cultivation in textile wastewater (TWW1 and TWW2), demonstrating effective COD reduction by 62.59% for TWW1, 46.68% for TWW2, which aligned with first-order kinetics. Nutrient removal rates showed phosphate reductions as 36.42% for TWW1 and 62.18% for TWW2, and ammonia reductions as 59.34% for TWW1, 69.31% for TWW2. Seed germination tests with Vigna radiata indicated enhanced growth using treated wastewater. This outcome suggests that there exists potential for their in use in irrigation. Increased lipid and carbohydrate content following treatment supports biofuel production. As the biofuel can be put to use, this contribute to the sustainability dimension of phycoremediation, especially in water management.94 Further development of this study into large-scale ponds, specifically using HRAPs, offers an alternative to traditional wastewater treatment methods. HRAPs can support the circular economy by utilizing reclaimed water and algal biomass. The study achieved average removal rates of 67% for total organic carbon, 76% for total nitrogen, 87% for NH4-N, 41% for total phosphorus, and 46% for PO4-P. Additionally, 12 contaminants of emerging concern (CECs) were identified in the influent and five in the effluent. The system removed 60% of naproxen, 51% of ibuprofen, 92% of methylparaben, 76% of 2,4-dihydroxybenzophenone, and 80% of oxybenzone.95 Another study explores using microalgae in high-rate algal ponds (HRAPs) for dual purposes, phycoremediation of wastewater and biomass production for biofuels. Removal efficiency increased to 18.9% compared with conventional wastewater treatment. It also emphasizes biomass harvesting and lipid extraction techniques.96 Another study investigated Botryococcus sp. biokinetics for NH4+ and PO43− removal from meat processing wastewater and NH4+ removal efficiency ranged from 89.74% to 99.03%, and PO43− removal efficiency ranged from 92.39% to 99.93%.97 Different open pond wastewater treatment systems using algae species were illustrated in Figure 3. Another study, investigated three native species a cyanobacterium Nostoc muscorum, diatom Navicula veneta, and green microalgae Chlorella vulgaris. It demonstrated the COD, TN, and TP removal efficiencies ranging from 85.7% to 99.8%. Navicula veneta met EU Directive standards for TN, TP, and COD in effluent, while Chlorella vulgaris partially complied. Navicula veneta exhibited the highest growth rate (0.88 ± 0.04 days−1), Chl-a-biomass yield (50.45 mg L−1), and removal efficiencies (96.9% TN, 99.8% TP, 95.7% COD).98

sec.title: Recent advancement in the phycoremediation of inland water reservoir
sec.p: Recent advancements in phycoremediation techniques for inland water reservoirs have shown promising developments. Innovations include the use of native microalgae species like Scenedesmus and Chlorella, which effectively remove nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus from water bodies. These techniques are enhanced through optimized growth conditions, including light and temperature regimes, to maximize biomass production and pollutant uptake. Furthermore, the integration of advanced monitoring and modeling tools has allowed for real-time assessment of water quality parameters and phycoremediation efficiency. Different integrated treatments and IOT monitoring systems are shown in Figure 4. A recent study with freshwater species such as Chlorella, Scenedesmus, Spirulina, and Chlamydomonas effectively remove heavy metals, nutrients, and organics through biosorption and bioaccumulation, and specifically, advances in PBR design continue to enhance the efficiency and feasibility of algal-based remediation systems.99 Another investigation with ex situ and in situ phycoremediation of Thirumanimuthar River water with Scenedesmus sp. reduced BOD and COD 27.83% and 23.30%, respectively.100 This wastewater treatment is not only limited to freshwater, but this research also extended to saline water. Many microalgae species are salt-tolerant, and commonly recognized species are Chlorophyta (e.g., Chlorella, Scenedesmus, and Dunaliella) and Cyanobacteria (e.g., Spirulina, Nostoc, Oscillatoria, and Anabaena), which exhibit substantial interspecific differences in desalination capacity.101 Furthermore, Arthrospira (Spirulina) sp and Macroalgae/Seaweeds have more salt tolerance and efficiently remove the various pollutants including nutrients, organic matter (COD/BOD), and heavy metals from industrial effluents such as dairy, textile, and petrochemical wastewater.23 Similarly, for industrial wastewater, remediation using Dictyosphaerium sp. attained 100% Mn2+ removal, surpassing free is 97.9%, acid-treated is 92.9%, and raw dried biomass yield is 88.7%.

sec.p: Raw dried and immobilized forms showed slightly lower Zn2+ removal of 96.6% and 93.9%.102 Chlorella vulgaris (NIES:227 strain) isolated from Ganga River, Haridwar, India was tested for dairy wastewaters treatment under different concentrations (0%, 50%, and 100%), temperatures (20°C, 25°C, and 30°C), and light intensities (2,000 lx, 3,000 lx, and 4,000 lx) through response surface methodology approach. It demonstrated significant reductions in BOD (96.65%) and COD (87.50%), alongside achieving maximum biomass of 1.757 g/L with 57.72% wastewater.103 Another advancement includes integrated phycoremediation technologies, which combine various treatment methods to optimize wastewater treatment using microalgae. These approaches include ozonation to enhance organic pollutant degradation, biochar for improved nutrient retention and biomass growth, advanced PBRs with real-time monitoring for optimal conditions, genetic engineering for enhancing microalgae capabilities, biorefinery concepts for valorizing biomass, and hybrid systems combining biological and chemical treatments.

An integrated method, combining ozonation and phycoremediation effectively treated raw tannery effluent with lab-scale ozone reactor operations at a low O3 flowrate (2 g/h) and it reported a significant improvement approximately 60% COD removal at an ozone consumption of 1.5 g O3/g, COD at pH 7.6. Also, it unveiled a substantial pollutant reduction of 60% color, 100% odor, 90% and 84% of COD and inorganic carbon, 100% PO4–P, 82% NH4+-N, 97% chromium, and 10% TDS.104 Another study with Arabidopsis thaliana extract to synthesize nearly 10 nm bio-based silver nanoparticles (n-AgO) without additional reducing agents. n-AgO modified polyethersulfone-polyvinylpyrrolidone (PES-PVP) membranes achieved flux recovery ratio FRR of 0.932 and reduced irreversible fouling in shrimp wastewater. Integration with Chlamydomonas sp. enhanced ammonia removal (87.94%) and total suspended solids (TSSs) exclusion (61.41%), with n-AgO membranes boosting overall remediation more than 94%.105 Further, Chlorella pyrenoidosa was cultivated and tested using both real sewage treatment plant wastewater and synthetic wastewater. The algae demonstrated significant nutrient and pollutant reduction capabilities, achieving reductions of 99.5% for nitrate, 94.2% for phosphate, and 87.1% for COD in STPW. In SWW, reductions were slightly lower but still substantial, with 99.2% for nitrate, 70.1% for phosphate, and 61.0% for COD. These results highlight C. pyrenoidosa’s effectiveness in wastewater remediation under varying conditions.106 Another integrated study, reported with Scenedesmus sp. ISTGA1 for municipal wastewater treatment and biodiesel production. It obtained strain enhancement wastewater pH (6.3 ± 0.5 to 8.3 ± 0.2) and dissolved oxygen (2.7-fold). It effectively removed heavy metals (ICP-AES) and organic contaminants (GC-MS). Maximum biomass and lipid production reached 1.81 g/L and 452 mg/L, respectively.107 Further, Tetraspora sp. NITD 18 used for phycoremediation of coke-oven wastewater, achieved maximum removal efficiencies of 79.02 ± 6.93% for phenol, 74.7 ± 5.07% for ammonia cal-N, and 80.4 ± 0.015% for cyanide at pH 7 with a 10% inoculum concentration highlights its potential for tertiary treatment of complex industrial wastewater.108 Further a combined phycoremediation with ultrasonication-irradiation treatment (iPUT) is found to enhance the sulfonamide antibiotics degradation. Chlamydomonas mexicana underwent variable ultrasonication treatments (20%–2 min to 40%–10 min) in single (SUT) and multiple-intermittent (IUT) modes. Sulfacetamide and sulfapyridine removal increased by > 1.7-fold and >1.95-fold with 20% SUT and IUT, respectively. Sulfamethazine removal peaked at 33.5% with 20% SUT and 27.5% with IUT. IUT significantly accelerated sulfamethoxazole and sulfadimethoxine degradation, achieving 9-fold and 12-fold increases in removal with 20% and 40% treatments, respectively.109 The nutrient removal capabilities of different algal species are summarized and categorized in Table 1.

sec.title: By-products from treated biomass and techno-economic study
sec.p: Although various technologies were employed for nutrient removal, each technique has its own advantages (Table 2). Therefore, to justify phycoremediation as an efficient method, a techno-economic analysis is needed to assess the financial feasibility and economic viability of using microalgae-based technologies for wastewater treatment and pollutant removal. Phycoremediation provides a sustainable and eco-friendly approach to wastewater treatment, effectively removing nitrogen, phosphorus, and metal ions and also yields the products of market interest. Pilot-scale integration of this approach remains unexplored despite demonstrated efficacy in treating swine wastewater. It involves analyzing the costs associated with algae cultivation, harvesting, processing, and product recovery against the benefits of reduced pollutant levels, resource recovery (such as biomass for biofuels or bioproducts), and potential revenue streams. Factors considered include capital investment, operational costs, energy requirements, market value of products, and environmental benefits. Microalgae’s efficient nutrient uptake from wastewater, achieving 71.2 ± 3.5% COD reduction, 81.9 ± 3.8% NH4+ removal, nearly 100.0% NO3− removal, and 94.1% PO43− removal, with Scenedesmus obliquus growing at a rate of 0.42 ± 0.02 L/d and reaching 0.88 ± 0.04 g/L biomass. Biomass yielded 26.5% lipids, 28.5% protein, and 27.5% carbohydrates by dry weight, with post-de-oiling, protein and carbohydrate yields at 25.3% and 21.4%, respectively. Further this study estimated a net profit of 16,885 US$·per year from phycoremediation, with a 14.8 years payback period.156 A recent study with Spirulina and Chlorella serves as valuable food protein supplements and feedstock for bioplastic production. Co-production of these proteins alongside biodiesel has been shown to significantly reduce overall production costs from $0.89/L to $0.59/L.157 The presence of heavy metals and other toxins in biomass may limit its use as a biofertilizer. Further, the remediation from diary wastewater using microalgae can produce biomass at $0.482/kg.158 Phycoremediation of potato industry wastewater (PIW) using Anabaena oryzae, Nostoc muscorum, and Spirulina platensis enabled simultaneous nutrient recovery and biomass generation, as well as the production of byproducts from biofertilizers Spi-PIW and Cyano-PIW. It is reducing chemical fertilizer needs by 25%–50% while promoting circular bioeconomy practices.68 Additionally, microalgae applications yield valuable by-products like pigments, polysaccharides, lipids, and proteins, with potential commercial benefits such as biodiesel, biohydrogen, bioelectricity, and biogas.159 Also, microalgal biomass co-digested with cow dung showed biomethane potential, yielding 618–925 mL/g VS with 48%–65% methane content.160 Chlorella sorokiniana demonstrated robust performance in phycoremediation, while effectively removing 90% of phosphate and 70% of nitrogen from the wastewater. The biomass harvested after phycoremediation from digestate was rich in volatile solids (95.4%) and proteins (59.5%). Furthermore, during monodigestion, the biomass exhibited a substantial biochemical methane potential (BMP) of 292 ± 10 mLNCH4 gVSadd-1. Integrating microalgae biomass into the anaerobic digestion process enhanced biogas production by up to 32.1%, highlighting its dual benefits in wastewater treatment and renewable energy production.161 An optimized study with N and P-supplemented wastewater under experimental cultivation of Chlorella sp. shows potential for producing 11,875 kg/year (31.3 kg/d) at a production cost of up to 18 USD/kg for dry biomass and 0.19 USD/bottle for concentrated biomass. Growth kinetics revealed substrate-dependent biomass reaching 1.25 g/L after 15 days, achieving 98% removal of available N and 20% of P.162
