sec.title: Special emphasis on mechanism of C and N uptake by algae cell
sec.p: The mechanisms of C and N uptake by algae cells involve several key processes. First, algae absorb carbon dioxide (CO2) from their surroundings through diffusion and actively transport it using carbonic anhydrase enzymes. The CO2 is then converted it into bicarbonate ions inside the cells of the algae. This is a key process in photosynthesis, as CO2 is fixed into organic carbon compounds, such as sugars.178 Regarding nitrogen uptake, algae mainly absorb nitrogen primarily in the form of ammonium (NH4+) and nitrate (NO3−) from their environment. For the uptake of ammonium, transport systems across the algal cell membrane are activated by proton gradients or ATP hydrolysis. Nitrate uptake, on the other hand, involves transport proteins that move nitrate ions into the cell. Once inside, these ions are reduced to ammonium or incorporated into amino acids and proteins. These uptake mechanisms are affected by environmental factors: nutrient availability, pH, light intensity, and temperature are some of the factors reported in the literature. Studies have been conducted to understand these processes, as they are vital for optimizing algae growth in various applications, including wastewater treatment, biofuel production, and bioremediation.179,180 For example, in one study involving FTIR analysis, 13C isotope incorporation was tracked all the way up to individual algal cells. The analysis revealed C- uptake and allocation across carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids. Spectral shifts in Spirogyra indicated significant cellulose incorporation at 1,160 cm−1, 1,108 cm−1, 1,080 cm−1, 1,048 cm−1, and 1,030 cm−1 peaks. Natural phytoplankton studies showed distinct C patterns; for instance, diatoms underwent observable changes in proteins and carbohydrates, while green algae and euglenoids showed fewer shifts.181 However, challenges such as culture contamination and prokaryotic overgrowth hinder productivity and stability in microalgal biorefineries. Automated online flow cytometry has been identified as a powerful tool for optimizing bioprocesses, as it provides real-time, high-resolution monitoring of microbial dynamics. One study has pioneered the application of this technique in microalgal ecosystems. In particular, it used fluorescence emissions to quantify and assess the diversity of Chlorella vulgaris, simultaneously, considering a range of concentrations (2.2–1,002.4 cells ·μL−1).182 The evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis led to reduced atmospheric CO2 level and increased O2 levels, restricting the activity of RUBISCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) during photosynthesis. To overcome this, algae and certain plants have developed CO2-concentrating mechanisms. These ensure greater availability of CO2 around RUBISCO, but variations have been noted by researchers among different algal groups.183

sec.title: C removal mechanism
sec.p: Algal strains utilize various mechanisms to remove carbon (C) from wastewater, all of which play crucial roles in cleaning and enhancing the quality of aquatic environments. Microalgae employ several mechanisms to remove carbon (C) from wastewater, contributing significantly to the purification of aquatic environments. In this section, key carbon removal mechanisms utilized by microalgae are highlighted.

sec.title: Photosynthesis
sec.p: CO2 fixation: microalgae utilize carbon dioxide (CO2) dissolved in wastewater as a carbon source for photosynthesis. Through the action of the enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RUBISCO), CO2 is incorporated into organic molecules, primarily sugars, within the algal cells.184,185 As a byproduct of photosynthesis, microalgae release oxygen (O2) into the wastewater. This process not only supports aerobic microbial activities but also enhances the dissolved oxygen levels in the water, crucial for the survival of aquatic organisms and overall ecosystem health.186

sec.title: Biochemical assimilation
sec.p: In addition to CO2, microalgae can also utilize and assimilate various organic carbon compounds present in wastewater. These may include sugars, organic acids, and other carbon-containing molecules that originate from organic pollutants or biomass decomposition.187 The carbon compounds taken up by microalgae are used for their cellular growth, maintenance, and energy production. The assimilation further helps in reducing the organic carbon load in wastewater, contributing to its purification.188 Certain microalgal species, especially coccolithophores and few green algae, have the ability to precipitate calcium carbonate (CaCO3) under specific environmental conditions. This process removes dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), such as bicarbonate ions (HCO3–) and carbonate ions (CO32–), from the wastewater.189 As part of the biomineralization process, the precipitation of calcium carbonate can occur either within or outside algal cells, depending on the algal species and the availability of calcium and carbonate ions in the wastewater. This mechanism contributes to both carbon removal and carbonate alkalinity regulation in aquatic systems.190

sec.title: Nitrogen removal mechanisms
sec.p: Microalgae assimilate nitrogen in wastewater by absorbing ammonium (NH4+) and nitrate (NO3−) through specialized transport proteins; NH4+ is directly incorporated into amino acids for protein synthesis,191 while NO3− is first reduced to NH4+ before assimilation. Additionally, nitrification-denitrification involves the microbial conversion of NH4+ to nitrite (NO2−) and nitrate (NO3−) by nitrifying bacteria, followed by reduction to nitrogen gas (N2) by denitrifying bacteria under anaerobic conditions.192 Some microalgae also actively exchange NH4+ across cell membranes, concentrating nitrogen intracellularly.193 Overall, microalgal systems achieve NH4+ removal efficiencies of 70%–90%, NO3− removal of 50%–90%, and NO2− removal of 20%–70%, depending on species, light intensity, and nutrient conditions, thereby enhancing nitrogen cycling and improving wastewater quality.194 Further, the nitrate reductase (NR) and glutamine synthetase–glutamate synthase (GS–GOGAT) pathways play significant roles in algal nitrogen assimilation and removal efficiency.195 The reduction of nitrate (NO3−) into nitrite (NO2−), followed by nitrite reductase converting it to ammonium (NH4+), which is then incorporated into amino acids through the GS–GOGAT cycle. In this process, GS converts NH4+ and glutamate into glutamine, and GOGAT regenerates glutamate using 2-oxoglutarate from carbon metabolism. Optimal coordination between pathways enhances nitrogen removal by facilitating rapid assimilation into cellular biomass, thereby tightly linking carbon fixation and nitrogen metabolism in various algal species.196

sec.title: Factors affecting algae-based nutrient removal
sec.p: Algae are photoautotrophic organisms that utilize light to produce essential chemical compounds for growth through the process of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis, stimulated by inorganic carbon supply, light, and temperature, enables the absorption of nutrients.197 Most of the studies were discussed with biomass production under the factors associated with the above. Research investigating the impact of light colors on PBRs using Chlamydomonas reinhardtii indicated that blue and red lights are less effective in generating algal biomass. The highest productivity was observed under warm white and yellow lights. The photoperiod, light intensity, and temperature play a major role in nutrient removal and value products. A research study with Ulva prolifera, conducted under a 12:12 light/dark cycle at 25°C and a light density of 400 μmol m−2 s−1, yields better performance. An increase in light density decreases chlorophyll fluorescence (Fv′/Fm′, NPQ, rETRmax).198 Another study with Coriandrum sativum L. reports an optimal efficiency and yield attained with a light intensity of 200 μmol m−2 s−1 and a 16-h photoperiod.199 Chlorella vulgaris in food processing wastewater treatment achieved 73% COD removal with a biomass yield of 0.44 g/L under a 12H:12H photoperiod. In contrast, a 24 h light cycle resulted in 75% COD removal with a biomass yield of 1.02 g/L.200 Furthermore, Lemna minor and Lemna trisulca exhibited greater growth under higher temperatures (25°C) and longer photoperiods (24 h). Lemna minor achieved maximum biomass and surface coverage under optimal conditions of 25°C and 12 h of light, indicating efficient resource utilization. In contrast, Lemna trisulca exhibited stable growth at lower temperatures 15°C, 12 h light, demonstrating better adaptability to variable physicochemical conditions.201 Scenedesmus sp. cultivated in an outdoor raceway pond achieved a maximum productivity of 12.5 ± 0.6 g m−2 d−1 during summer, which is 30% higher than that observed in winter, attributed to the photoperiod. Seasonal light fluctuations also affect nutrient uptake, with complete ammoniacal nitrogen and 85% phosphorus removal, demonstrating effective coupling of photosynthetic activity with wastewater remediation.202 Additionally, supplementing yellow light with blue light enhanced growth and overall culture capability.203 A recent study reported that the biomass production of Desmodesmus sp. cultures increased with light intensity. However, raising the light intensity from 150 to 300 μE m−2 s−1 did not significantly affect the biomass of Chlorella vulgaris and Scenedesmus obliquus, which were approximately 0.6 and 0.8 g/L, respectively, at 150 μE m−2 s−1 after one week. Thus, 150 μE m−2 s−1 was optimal for biomass production in these two species.204 Light significantly influences algal growth and nutrient utilization efficiency. In controlled indoor systems, artificial light sources can enhance the photosynthetic activity of microalgae. Microalgae photosynthetic systems are most efficient in the blue (around 400 nm) and red (600–700 nm) regions of the light spectrum, optimizing the utilization of nitrogen and phosphorus from wastewater.205 Red light, in particular, stimulates algal growth. Although using artificial light increases the cost of wastewater treatment, light-emitting diode (LED) technology, with a longer lifespan and lower electricity consumption, makes the use of artificial light sources more viable. This enhances photosynthetic activity and nutrient uptake from the water body, improving the overall efficiency of the treatment process.206 Many studies have demonstrated specific light preferences among different microalgae species, Spirulina platensis exhibited a 38% increase in growth rate under red light. Optimal productivity for Chlorella vulgaris was achieved using green light and research on high-density cultures of Scenedesmus bijuga indicated that green light, which is weakly absorbed, enhances photosynthetic efficiency.207,208 In open water systems, light availability varies with depth and can be limited by dense algae and other microorganisms. Proper water circulation is crucial for optimal microalgae exposure, as prolonged exposure to intense surface sunlight can damage photosystem II and reduce photosynthetic efficiency.209 In addition to light, temperature has a strong influence on algae growth in various bioremediation systems. It has been found that algae species thrive best when the temperature ranges between 15°C and 30 °C. However, closed PBRs exposed to sunlight can exceed 40 °C, so cooling systems need to be installed to maintain optimal growth conditions, which in turn increases treatment costs.210,211 At approximately 36 °C, algal growth rates reportedly decrease by 7%–10%—heat stress is thus a detriment to growth. Arctic strains of Chlorella were found to show optimum growth between 6°C and 20 °C (μ = 0.19–0.22 days–1), but tolerated growth up to 30 °C. Another study reported that the tolerable temperature range of Chlorella vulgaris can tolerate temperatures is from 15°C to 40 °C. Overall, microalgae species grow optimally at around 15 °C, with growth inhibition occurring when temperatures exceed their optimal range by 2°C–4°C.212,213 The pH level plays a crucial role in algae-based wastewater treatment systems because it affects many biochemical and physiological processes within the algae cells. In general, algae grow better and take up nutrients more efficiently in neutral to slightly alkaline conditions. For example, Chlorella spp. typically grows best in a pH range between 6.5 and 8.5.214 Additionally, studies indicate that the pH level affects the solubility and availability of nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, in wastewater. At higher pH levels, ammonia (NH3/NH4+) mostly exists in the toxic ammonia (NH3) form, which can inhibit algal growth. Conversely, at lower pH, the ammonium ion (NH4+) becomes more dominant and is generally less harmful to the cells.215 This parameter influences the composition of algal biomass as well, including its lipid content, protein synthesis, and carbohydrate production. For instance, under certain pH conditions, algae tend to increase lipid accumulation, which is beneficial for biodiesel production. However, it is still important to regulate temperature and nutrient concentrations, so that optimum conditions for algal growth and nutrient removal efficiency can be established.216,217,218 In open pond systems, pH alone is insufficient to control pathogen levels effectively. Factors like temperature, dissolved oxygen, and solar radiation must also be managed, as they are closely interconnected and can directly influence pathogen concentrations. Increased solar radiation, for instance, can reduce pathogens in water or stimulate algal growth.219,220 CO2 is a fundamental substrate for photosynthesis in microalgae. During this process, microalgae use CO2 together with water and light energy to produce carbohydrates and release oxygen. In wastewater treatment applications, microalgae remove nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus from the water; simultaneously, they produce biomass, which can be harvested and processed for use in various applications such as biofuels, bioplastics, and animal feed additive.221 During wastewater treatment, algae rely on sources of inorganic carbon, primarily supplied through the aerobic respiration of bacteria within the wastewater. This process releases CO2, which algae utilize for photosynthesis, thereby promoting their growth.222 Additionally, researchers have suggested supplementing with extra CO2 as a proactive measure to enhance algal biomass production. Another critical source of inorganic carbon is bicarbonate ions (HCO3−); these ions are formed during the hydrolysis of CO2, which significantly enhances algal growth rates during water treatment.223

In addition to cultivation factors, the use of nanoparticles, such as magnetic nanoparticles and metal oxide nanoparticles like CeO2, ZnO, Fe3O4, and Al2O3, plays a significant role in enhancing the removal of contaminants. Biochar-loaded nano zero-valent iron (nZVI/BC) improved nZVI stability and effectively removed Microcystis aeruginosa while reducing toxicity to E. coli compared to bare nZVI, where strong ROS-induced oxidative stress caused rapid cell inactivation, indicating that nanoparticle surface modification can balance reactivity and environmental safety.224 In some cases, nanoparticles and pharmaceuticals persist in the water even after treatment. Its presence in a water body for a prolonged duration primarily affects the ecological system due to its toxicity.225 Further, it damages algae and other aquatic organisms, leading to bioaccumulation, trophic transfer up the food chain, and lasting ecosystem damage.226 A study discusses that ZnO has significantly toxic effects on microalgae Chlorella vulgaris and Scenedesmus obliquus, with this toxicity mechanism involving the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which results in the release of toxic zinc ions (ZN2+) and causes physical damage, disrupting essential physiological processes like photosynthesis and nutrient uptake.227 Further study with ZnO and Fe2O3 nanoparticles exhibited dose-dependent toxicity toward Chlorella vulgaris, causing growth inhibition, oxidative stress, and cell membrane damage, with significantly lower IC50 values (0.258 and 12.99 mg L−1) than their bulk forms. The enhanced toxicity of nanoforms highlights their greater ecological risk to aquatic microalgae and potential disruption of aquatic ecosystems.227 Binary exposure of Chlorella vulgaris to ZnO nanoparticles and tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) caused severe cellular damage, oxidative stress, and chlorophyll reduction, while humic acid reduced this synergistic toxicity highlighting that nanoparticle–pollutant interactions can amplify ecological risks and disrupt aquatic primary productivity.228 Genetic/metabolic engineering of algal wild types is an emerging area of research in bioremediation. The limitation of wild strain for pollutant removal is overcome by genetic engineering approach. Genetic modification through plasmid conjugation (overexpressing the CPA1, CPA2, and CPA3 genes) and random mutagenesis (RM) have been employed to improve the salt removal efficiency of microalgae. These approaches also enhance self-flocculation ability and promote higher lipid accumulation, thereby improving overall performance.229 Further, microalgal Metallothioneins and Phytochelatins are majorly used for heavy metal removal. Genetically modified Chlamydomonas reinhardtii and co-cultured with engineered Pseudomonas stutzeri attained superior N2 and NH3 removal through improved CO2/O2 exchange and nutrient cycling.230

sec.title: Challenges and recommendations
sec.p: Using phycoremediation to clean water streams and remove nutrients can be a very cost-effective compared to using conventional methods, although large-scale cultivation still poses certain challenges. One of the challenges is selecting suitable microalgae among a million species to identify strains, specifically for industrial and WWT applications; here, high-through-put screening can be helpful. The screening process will then guide the design of algal groups that can adapt to diverse wastewater compositions. During phycoremediation, reducing the hydraulic retention time (HRT) is crucial, as it directly influences the system’s energy efficiency per cubic meter of treated water. To reduce HRT, the integration of attached cultivation with fast-growing microalgae has been proposed as a potential approach, which also reduces operational costs. Another reason for recommending this technique is that research has shown that there is scope for further advancements in, among other aspects, strain selection, consortia design, and operational efficiencies. Like any innovation, algae cultivation also faces challenges in terms of productivity, energy consumption, and economics. For example, the solid-liquid separation process can be quite energy-intensive. For effective dewatering, separation, and drying, specific solutions need to be synthesized. Additionally, cultivation, harvesting, and biomass extraction all contribute to the costs. One factor that favors this technique is that industries worldwide often have ample space available. Establishing large-scale algae cultivation units near water reservoirs is another recommendation that has frequently come up in studies. Additionally, for heavy metal removal, the authors recommend incorporating a separate filtration system, which would further enhance the overall water treatment efficiency. These approaches effectively utilize existing industrial areas while leveraging the natural capacity of algae to purify wastewater, thereby supporting both environmental objectives and regulatory compliance. In the long run, investing in R&D to improve and optimize indigenous algae species can be a long-term strategy for reducing costs, while the by-products generated during wastewater treatment could support national economies. Local algal species are naturally adaptable, and cultivation conditions can be optimized to maximize this trait. Doing so not only improves nutrient removal but also increases biomass output, from which valuable by-products such as proteins, lipids, enzymes, and vitamins can be obtained. Additionally, genetic/metabolic engineering of algal wild types is an emerging area of research in bioremediation. The limitation of the wild strain for pollutant removal is overcome by a genetic engineering approach. Overall, integrating advanced cultivation techniques with targeted genetic engineering strategies can greatly enhance the capabilities of native algae, thereby paving the way for sustainable solutions for inland water remediation in the future.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This review presents a holistic discussion of inland and wastewater nutrient removal through phycoremediation, a process that utilizes nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, and minerals as nutrients, while also removing contaminants from water bodies. Key insights derived from this review are presented below. Different algal species (e.g., Chlorella, Scenedesmus, Spirulina, Phaeodactylum tricornutum, Nannochloropsis, Dunaliella, and Euglena) are known for their effectiveness in wastewater treatment. These species adeptly extract nutrients, such as nitrogen and phosphorus, significantly aiding in water purification efforts. An integrated ozonation and phycoremediation in treating tannery effluent, achieving 60%–80% COD removal with 60% color removal and 100% odor removal. Among the reactors, fluidized-bed reactors with Chlorella vulgaris or Scenedesmus abundans for treatment of secondary effluent showed efficient removal of TP and TN. Under optimized experimental conditions, the microalgal consortia exhibited 86% phosphate, 70% nitrogen, and 70% P removal, along with concurrent production of biomass and lutein from tolerant biomass. As a biorefinery approach, the lipid content from treated algal biomass can serve as a parent material for high-quality biodiesel production, which contains desirable fatty acids such as C16:0, C16:1, C18:1, C18:2, and C18:3. Algae have the ability to utilize C, N, and P, which are commonly found in inland water, and therefore, inland water/wastewater from different sources can be bioremediated by algae at a point source in an environmentally benign approach. However, genetic/metabolic engineering of wild-type algae represents a rapidly advancing area in bioremediation research. Through targeted genetic modifications, the inherent limitations of natural strains in C and N removal, as well as other pollutant removal, can be effectively overcome. As a path to future study, advanced genome-editing tools, such as CRISPR-Cas9, TALENs, and RNAi, enable the efficient regulation or knockout of genes to enhance nutrient uptake and increase stress tolerance. Additionally, overexpression of antioxidant and osmoprotectant genes strengthens cellular defense mechanisms under adverse wastewater conditions.
